title: Apollo launches $11 billion private credit platform, backed by Abu Dhabi
description: Apollo Global Management has launched a European private credit platform with more than 10 billion euros ($11.2 billion) of lending capacity, backed b
body: Apollo Global Management has launched a European private credit platform with more than 10 billion euros ($11.2 billion) of lending capacity, backed by several blue-chip investors, including the Abu Dhabi Investment Council (ADIC).The European Credit Company will invest in performing credit across the large and mid-market sectors, including corporate and asset-backed lending, as well as lending to real-asset owners in infrastructure and real estate.The venture is led by Giacomo Petrobelli, serving as chief executive officer, and Christian Meissner, its chairman.Stock Chart IconStock chart iconApollo Global Management.Petrobelli said Apollo's ECC aims to capitalize on a "generational opportunity" to finance Europe's long-term growth agenda using global pools of capital. Apollo partners with ADIC The venture's backing from ADIC comes a week after Apollo agreed to buy a nearly 10% stake in Mubadala Capital, the alternative asset manager subsidiary of Mubadala Investment Co., Abu Dhabi's sovereign wealth fund.Other strategic partners in the new platform include European insurance group Athora, Japanese lender Norinchukin Bank, Standard Chartered and Aranda Principal Strategies, a U.S. credit investor, Apollo said in an announcement."We aim to build ECC into a premier pan-European credit platform, focused exclusively on the region, with deep local relationships, differentiated sourcing and flexible solutions that span all credit types," said Petrobelli."The Global Industrial Renaissance is creating tremendous financing needs around the world that are acutely felt in Europe, whether it's energy transition and transmission, defense, or digital and traditional infrastructure," added Apollo president Jim Zelter.

schema.headline: Apollo launches $11 billion private credit platform, backed by Abu Dhabi

title: Rubio says Trump wants to end Iran war 'peacefully' even as both sides prepare for strikes
description: US Secretary of State Marco Rubio speaks during the Freedom 250 reception at the Jio World Convention Centre in Mumbai on October 20, 2026. Kylie Coop
body: US Secretary of State Marco Rubio speaks during the Freedom 250 reception at the Jio World Convention Centre in Mumbai on October 20, 2026. Kylie Cooper | Afp | Getty ImagesU.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio said President Donald Trump would like to resolve the Iranian war "diplomatically," and prefers not to use military force. Speaking over the weekend, Rubio told reporters that "He [Trump] hasn't made a decision...what the president expresses to you is incredible confidence that if we needed to do something militarily, we would have the ability to do it, and we really we have everything we need to be successful. But we would prefer to do it peacefully."The remarks come as reports suggest both sides are gearing up for additional military strikes after the midterm elections. On Saturday, Iranian Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei called for Tehran's armed forces to meet "any level or type of threat" with "an immediate, impactful, and geographically unrestricted response."He also ordered that its military database be updated so that "all kinds of physical and non-physical assets of the U.S.-Zionist enemy are brought within the reach of the Armed Forces," referring to U.S. and Israeli forces.Washington has not explicitly stated it plans to resume attacks on Iran, but reports from The Wall Street Journal and The New York Times indicate the U.S. is preparing for possible renewed military actions after the Nov. 3 midterm elections. On Sunday, Trump told the Right Side Broadcasting Network. "We've had such a victory, and we'll put it away very soon, one way or the other.""Either they'll make a deal, or we'll just end it," he added.Iran targets U.K. intelligenceOn Sunday, Iran's foreign ministry designated the U.K.'s Military Intelligence Services as a "hostile group" and accused the Royal Navy and Air Force of supporting "terrorist organizations."In a Telegram post, the ministry said that the move was a response to what it called London's "malicious" actions, including the designation of the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps as a "terrorist organization."Tehran has separately accused the U.K. of participating in the U.S.-Iran war by allowing American forces access to British military and logistical bases.The U.K. had allowed U.S. forces to use RAF Fairford and Diego Garcia for what were described as "defensive" strikes on Iran, according to the BBC.

schema.headline: Rubio says Trump wants to end Iran war 'peacefully' even as both sides prepare for strikes

title: Prediction market traders now see nearly 75% chance of Democrats winning the Senate
description: A Kalshi billboard displaying US Senate midterm election odds in New York, US, on Friday, Oct. 16, 2026.Michael Nagle | Bloomberg | Getty ImagesMoment
body: A Kalshi billboard displaying US Senate midterm election odds in New York, US, on Friday, Oct. 16, 2026.Michael Nagle | Bloomberg | Getty ImagesMomentum for Democrats is building on Kalshi, with traders on Monday seeing a 74% chance of the party winning control of the U.S. Senate — the highest odds seen for the party on the platform since the market first opened. The higher odds come after The New York Times reported Sunday that a poll it conducted with Siena University found Democrats are leading in several battleground states, strengthening Democrats' path to a possible Senate majority. The contract asks "Who will control the Senate?" and will be verified by the Library of Congress after Tuesday's vote. Since it opened in 2024, Republicans dominated the market for Senate control in 2026. The gap between the parties' odds narrowed shortly after the U.S. and Israel first launched strikes on Iran on Feb. 28, though the chances for Republican control jumped up to 60% in July before reversing in mid-September. Markets on separate Senate races have also seen major movement in favor of Democratic candidates in the last 24 hours. Traders on Kalshi now see a 74% chance of Democrats winning the Senate race in Texas, up from 68.4%, over the past 24 hours. The market on the Senate race in Iowa jumped to 50% from 42% on Polymarket in favor of Democrats. In Kansas, which has not elected a Democratic U.S. senator since 1932, odds of Democratic candidate Adam Hamilton winning over Republican Roger Marshall are up to 63% from 52%.Odds and gambling platforms do not use methodologies used by traditional political polling, and therefore are not substitutes for political polls.Disclosure: CNBC and Kalshi have a commercial relationship that includes customer acquisition and a minority investment.

title: South Korea targets 'world's highest performance' sovereign AI model in record new budget
description: NEW YORK, UNITED STATES - SEPTEMBER 22: President of South Korea Lee Jae Myung addresses the 81st session of the United Nations General Assembly, whic
body: NEW YORK, UNITED STATES - SEPTEMBER 22: President of South Korea Lee Jae Myung addresses the 81st session of the United Nations General Assembly, which brings together leaders and senior representatives of UN member states in New York, United States, on September 22, 2026.  Anadolu | Anadolu | Getty ImagesSouth Korean President Lee Jae Myung unveiled the country's largest ever budget on Monday, pledging to "boldly invest in AI and future growth engines."Speaking to the National Assembly on Monday, Lee said total spending for 2027 would rise 12.8% to 820.9 trillion won ($610.14 billion), including 21.3 trillion won for semiconductors, physical AI and AI data centers — nearly double the 2026 level.A separate 4.7 trillion won will go toward developing a sovereign AI model with what Lee described as the "world's highest performance."The government also plans to invest heavily into talent, including training 2,000 specialists to "lead semiconductor design and the regional semiconductor industry," while expanding AI education for students, job seekers and existing workers.South Korea has set up university "contract departments," where students can enroll in company-linked degrees that offer pathways to jobs at firms like Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix before graduation.Companies help design courses, provide financial support and recruit qualifying graduates.The record spending plan comes as the International Monetary Fund forecasts South Korea's economy will grow 3.3% in 2026, its fastest pace since the post pandemic rebound in 2021. Lee said the higher spending would result in "virtually no net increase in government debt," with newly issued bonds used to repay existing debt.The budget also increases spending on defense and social security spending for the youth. Defense expenditure is set to rise 8.2% to 73.3 trillion won."We will rapidly transform into a smart, elite, and powerful military by establishing a hybrid manned and unmanned system based on AI, robots, and drones," Lee said.South Korea's strong economic growth has been driven largely by semiconductor exports as global demand for computing power rises with the AI boom.Exports surged 93.7% from a year earlier to a record $115.3 billion in October, according to data released Sunday by the Korea Customs Service. Shipments totaled $930 billion in the first 10 months of 2026, surpassing the $900 billion mark for the first time. The country posted a $42.5 billion trade surplus in October, with imports rising 36% year on year to $72.8 billion.Lee said South Korea was within reach of $1 trillion in annual exports, citing strong performance in key industries including semiconductors.

schema.headline: South Korea targets 'world's highest performance' sovereign AI model in record new budget

title: Canada-India $5.5 billion bank takeover attracts opposition from workers, politicians
description: GERMANY - 2026/05/20: In this photo illustration, the logo of company Fairfax Financial Holdings Limited is displayed on a smartphone in front of abst
body: GERMANY - 2026/05/20: In this photo illustration, the logo of company Fairfax Financial Holdings Limited is displayed on a smartphone in front of abstract background on computer screen. Sopa Images | Lightrocket | Getty ImagesCanadian firm Fairfax Financial Holdings' proposed $5.5 billion takeover of IDBI Bank is facing pushback from employees of the Indian state-owned lender and political parties in the country.On Sunday, the United Forum of IDBI Officers and Employees called for a two-day "nationwide" strike against the sale of the bank to Fairfax. The workers' union also expressed "grave concerns" about the transparency of the sale and valuation process, according to a post on X. It is demanding that the government "cancel the privatization process" and instead focus on strengthening the bank while protecting public investment and employees' interests. Last week, Rahul Gandhi, India's leader of the opposition, extended support to the IDBI Bank employee unions opposing the takeover by Fairfax. "Public banks are not assets to be sold off, they are tools to build the nation," Gandhi said in a statement on Thursday. He added that the sale of over 60% stake in IDBI Bank to Fairfax goes against the commitment of previous governments to hold a 51% stake in the state-owned lender.Nirmala Sitharaman, India's finance minister, in her response said the public sector bank was handed to the government in "poor shape" and was revived through "professionalism, prudence" and recapitalization of more than 250 billion rupees ($2.6 billion)."The IDBI Bank is now poised for its next phase of growth," the finance minister said. The government has previously said that the next phase of growth will be driven by a strategic investor.The Indian government on Oct.14 said the sale of over 60% of the share in IDBI will mark the largest foreign direct investment transaction in India's financial sector. Fairfax made a bid to pay 81 rupees per share for IDBI against the average fair value set at 75.99 rupees apiece.On Monday, shares of IDBI opened at around 79 rupees per share.However, Indian media outlet Businessworld on Thursday reported that government officials had suppressed the valuation of IDBI to make Fairfax's offer seem attractive. The Ministry of Finance has defended its procedure, adding that the bidding process was a "double blind" as the bidder did not know the valuation and the valuators did not see the bids.The Indian government has been divesting stakes this year as it pushes to keep the country's growth engine running amid deepening fiscal pressures. It sold shares in several companies, including Cochin Shipyard, Indian Railways Finance Corp, NHPC and Coal India. In August, it got $3.3 billion for a 6.5% stake in the country's top life insurer, Life Insurance Corporation of India.

schema.headline: Canada-India $5.5 billion bank takeover attracts opposition from workers, politicians

title: Texas governor race tightens in prediction markets, but Abbott remains favored
description: Republican Texas Gov. Greg Abbott, left, and Democratic gubernatorial candidate Gina Hinojosa.Getty ImagesPolitical observers are watching the Texas g
body: Republican Texas Gov. Greg Abbott, left, and Democratic gubernatorial candidate Gina Hinojosa.Getty ImagesPolitical observers are watching the Texas gubernatorial election for signs of an artificial intelligence data center backlash in the 2026 U.S. midterm elections on Tuesday, and prediction market traders see growing odds of the Democratic candidate pulling off an upset.Gov. Greg Abbott, a Republican seeking a fourth term, has a 60% chance of beating Democratic state Rep. Gina Hinojosa on Tuesday, according to speculators on platform Kalshi. Hinojosa's odds to win have jumped from 8% in mid-July to 40% on Monday, with many of those gains coming in recent weeks as a series of polls have shown the race to be tightening. On Polymarket, Hinojosa has seen her odds jump from as low as 5% in late July to 39% on Monday. Contracts are resolved using data from the Texas Secretary of State's office. Odds and gambling platforms do not use methodologies used by traditional political polling, and therefore are not substitutes for political polls.Hinojosa is seeking to be the first Democratic governor in Texas in more than 30 years. She has used Abbott's previous support for data center development in the state as an attack against the incumbent.In November 2025, Abbott touted a $40 billion investment by Google — which included bringing three new data centers to the state — by saying that Texas will be the "epicenter of AI development." But Abbott has changed his tune as voters' opinion of data centers has soured over the past year. Abbott in August ordered an audit of data centers that sought to connect to the state's grid, and then in September halted the approval of all data center-related permits until an audit of the existing waitlist is conducted.Hinojosa is running on an immediate data center moratorium until the legislature puts guardrails on the industry, according to her campaign website. In-person early voting in Texas concluded on Friday, and more than 7.7 million Texans have already cast their ballots. Disclosure: CNBC and Kalshi have a commercial relationship that includes customer acquisition and a minority investment.

title: Alaska Sen. Sullivan says he'll accept election results, slams Peltola campaign’s reported recruitment of 2nd Sullivan
description: Sen. Dan Sullivan (R-AK), and Democratic US Senate candidate Mary Peltola.ReutersAlaska Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan said Sunday he would accept the r
body: Sen. Dan Sullivan (R-AK), and Democratic US Senate candidate Mary Peltola.ReutersAlaska Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan said Sunday he would accept the results of Tuesday's midterm elections, while slamming Democratic candidate Mary Peltola's campaign for reportedly recruiting Dan J. Sullivan to run as a spoiler. "No, I'm going to accept the election results," Sullivan said on CNN's "State of the Union" when asked whether he would accept the results only if he wins. President Donald Trump's Department of Justice has sued Alaska, demanding the state not certify the election if the incumbent Republican loses.The lawsuit cites theoretical voter confusion over the appearance of the second Sullivan on the ballot, which DOJ says could siphon votes away from the incumbent Republican Sullivan and benefit Peltola. Alaska's Senate race is rated as a "toss-up" by the nonpartisan Cook Political Report with Amy Walter, and Peltola holds a slight edge in the polling average compiled by FiftyPlusOne. Peltola has repeatedly denied any involvement with the second Sullivan. However, The New York Times reported last week that her campaign was directly involved with recruiting Dan J. Sullivan, a retired schoolteacher, to run as a spoiler. Ballot-stacking is typically not illegal, and both parties have used it in past elections. Still, Alaska Gov. Mike Dunleavy ordered a criminal investigation into the alleged scheme. Alaska's Supreme Court upheld Dan J. Sullivan's place on the ballot during an earlier legal challenge.Sullivan on CNN said that the Times report shows Peltola's campaign, along with the Democratic Senate campaign arm, "recognizing they couldn't run on their record, so they had to cheat.""I think a lot of Alaskans, even Democrats, are thinking she is not fit for office; she's continually lying to the Alaskan people, and I guarantee you she's lying right now," Sullivan said. Peltola denied any knowledge of the alleged scheme to draft a second Sullivan in an interview with KTUU on Friday. "I honestly have no idea," Peltola said. "This is offensive to me on a number of different levels; first of all, this is Alaska, we're not in the business of tricking each other up here." "I've won statewide before, on my own merits, without any tricks involved; I know I can win again," she said. The stakes of the Alaska race are high. Democrats need to flip four seats while holding all currently Democratic seats to win a Senate majority. Alaska has emerged as a top opportunity for one of those flips. The midterms will determine which party controls Congress for the remainder of Trump's term in the White House.

schema.headline: Alaska Sen. Sullivan says he'll accept election results, slams Peltola campaign’s reported recruitment of 2nd Sullivan

title: Oracle files to sell $20 billion in new stock, bonds to finance AI buildout
description: The Oracle logo is displayed on a building at an Oracle campus in Redwood Shores, California, Sept. 10, 2025.Justin Sullivan | Getty ImagesOracle file
body: The Oracle logo is displayed on a building at an Oracle campus in Redwood Shores, California, Sept. 10, 2025.Justin Sullivan | Getty ImagesOracle filed plans on Monday to issue new stock and more debt to finance its artificial intelligence buildout. The hyperscaler will sell $10 billion in common stock and $10 billion in senior notes, according to filings with the Securities and Exchange Commission. While the fundraising was already outlined at an investor day last week, shares tumbled 8.8% Monday. "This seems to be exactly what they previewed," said Rob Oliver, senior research analyst at Baird. "So I'm not sure why the market is freaking about it."Oracle said it plans to use the proceeds for general corporate purposes, which may include capital expenditures, repayments of debt and future investments. Stock Chart IconStock chart iconOracle's one-day performanceThe hyperscaler's stock initially bounced after last Wednesday's investor day, when Oracle also issued a revenue forecast of at least $225 billion for fiscal 2030. At the time Oracle also said it was limiting its additional capital market funding for the fiscal 2027 to 2030 investment cycle to that $20 billion. "This is a major relief given concerns about the state of debt markets and the cost of capital (although UBS has argued that these debt market concerns have been over-stated)," UBS analyst Karl Keirstead said in a note on Thursday.Oracle plans to turn to vendor financing, customer-provided hardware and customer prepayments to help it transition to positive free cash flow, which it expects to reach in the second half of 2028.Stock and bonds in Oracle, co-founded by former CEO Larry Ellison, have been under pressure amid growing investor concerns about the massive amount of debt being taken on to fund AI infrastructure. Oracle shares are down 33% in 2026 and 50% over the past 12 months. The yield on its investment-grade 4.95% bond due in 2031 is currently 7.276%. The sentiment shift is also seen in Oracle's five-year credit default swaps, which are insurance against default. The spread sits at 292, up 265% in one year. That's more in line with a high-end junk bond rating, according to S&P Global Market Intelligence's Gavan Nolan. Oracle's five-year credit default swaps on Nov. 2, 2026While still an investment-grade credit, Oracle was downgraded by S&P to a BBB- in July, one rating level above high yield. It has $125.34 billion in debt, as of Aug. 31, with the bulk in senior notes.What ultimately matters for Oracle is execution, Pat Nerney, head of investment solutions at Dynasty Financial Partners, said in an email to CNBC Monday."Can they do what they say they are going to do? We view this as the narrative across the AI space," he said. "If this gets executed according to plans laid out, they will be rewarded. If they have to come back to market in the back half of '27 after telling everyone this was the last of the capital needed ... look out."— CNBC's Seema Mody and Ari Levy contributed reporting.

schema.headline: Oracle files to sell $20 billion in new stock, bonds to finance AI buildout

title: Fake nuclear warnings in Ukraine as Moscow, Kyiv report separate cyberattacks on emergency apps
description: Ukraine's air force said Sunday its Air Alert app had been compromised after it reportedly sent false warnings of nuclear and chemical threats in Kyiv
body: Ukraine's air force said Sunday its Air Alert app had been compromised after it reportedly sent false warnings of nuclear and chemical threats in Kyiv and other areas.The app briefly displayed alerts for nuclear and chemical incidents as well as warnings of street fighting, according to Reuters. The air force said unauthorized persons had interfered with the app's operation and that it had temporarily disabled push notifications."There is no radiation threat! Stay calm, follow our messages on our channel," the air force said on Telegram, according to a translation.Two hours later, Russia's Ministry for Emergency Situations said its mobile app had been subject to "a massive cyberattack, allowing attackers to send fake information to the public."It was not immediately clear if the incidents were linked. CNBC has reached out to Russian and Ukrainian authorities for comment. Local ceasefire expires in Oleshky, KhersonThe alleged cyberattacks come as Russia and Ukraine continue to trade strikes on each other's territories and infrastructure. Overnight, a local ceasefire in the devastated Russian-occupied city of Oleshky and surrounding areas in the Kherson region, near the Crimean Peninsula, expired. The temporary pause in fighting allowed humanitarian aid to enter the city and the evacuation of hundreds of people who had been trapped largely without access to food, water, electricity and medicine. It was the longest local ceasefire since the full-scale invasion began in early 2022, and both parties appeared to have honored the pause until it ended at midnight Moscow time. KHERSON, UKRAINE - OCTOBER 28: During a ceasefire, a man on a bicycle rides past residential buildings previously damaged by Russian strikes on October 28, 2026 in Kherson, Ukraine. (Photo by Ivan Antypenko/Suspilne Ukraine/JSC "UA:PBC"/Global Images Ukraine via Getty Images)Global Images Ukraine | Global Images Ukraine | Getty ImagesOn Monday morning, local media reported that Russian forces had struck a hospital in central Kherson, while Ukraine's General Staff of Armed Forces said Moscow had used the ceasefire to reinforce its military positions in the city."During the ceasefire, the rotation of Russian units, the fortification of positions, the expansion of anti-drone measures along roads and increased logistics activity, including the delivery of ammunition, were recorded," the military body said early Monday.On Sunday, President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said October had been the deadliest month for Russia since the invasion began in 2022.Over the past month, Russia lost 54,400 troops killed or badly wounded, "a record for any month of the full-scale war," Zelenskyy said, adding that Ukraine's Defense Forces liberated 96.2 square kilometers (37.1 square miles) of Ukrainian land in October – 10.4 square kilometers more than Russia captured during that time.

schema.headline: Fake nuclear warnings in Ukraine as Moscow, Kyiv report separate cyberattacks on emergency apps

title: Judge tosses DOJ case against ex-FBI officials accused of lying about Hunter Biden probe
description: Deputy Assistant Director for Counterterrorism at the FBI Nikki Floris, testifies before the House Judiciary Committee hearing on Capitol Hill in Wash
body: Deputy Assistant Director for Counterterrorism at the FBI Nikki Floris, testifies before the House Judiciary Committee hearing on Capitol Hill in Washington, Oct. 22, 2019.Susan Walsh | APA federal judge on Monday blasted the Department of Justice for "weaponization" as he dismissed its case accusing two former FBI officials of lying to Congress about investigations into Hunter Biden, multiple news outlets reported.Magistrate Judge Zia Faruqui, in a hearing in U.S. District Court in Washington, reportedly tore into the DOJ over its "slapdash job" prosecuting ex-officials Nikki Floris and Bradley Benavides, saying he was "deeply troubled by what has happened here."Faruqui said the government lacked probable cause and failed to present evidence that the officials' statements before the House Judiciary Committee in 2023 were knowingly false, MS NOW reported. He also accused the DOJ of wrongly rushing the case ahead of the midterm election. The situation "cannot be described as anything other than weaponization," he said, according to MS NOW.The judge even apologized to the government's lawyers, calling it "incredibly unfair" that they were assigned to defend the flawed case."This does not feel like an investigation," Faruqui reportedly added. "It feels like a broken one-wish willow obsession."The DOJ, in response to an email sent to its press office, said it "disagrees" with the decision. "We are evaluating all options but cannot comment further on an ongoing criminal investigation," the agency said in response to CNBC. "The Department's actions will continue to be guided by the facts, the evidence, and the law – not politics."Attorneys for Floris and Benavides praised the judge's decision outside the courthouse later Monday morning."This case should never have been brought. The government had no case, as the judge just laid out," a lawyer for Floris said, slamming the prosecution as a "spaghetti-at-the-wall, Hunter-Biden-conspiracy fever dream."A lawyer for Benavides said they hope the DOJ will not try to keep the case alive by seeking an indictment before a grand jury "where they get to be behind closed doors and get to shape the narrative, and we are unable to present our side."The DOJ did not take that step when they unveiled the allegations against Floris and Benavides on Oct. 23. Rather, despite the alleged misconduct taking place years earlier, prosecutors acquired a criminal complaint, which only requires a judge's signature. Criminal complaints are often used to obtain arrest warrant in situations where prosecutors need to move quickly.Faruqui had flagged that circumstance as unusual, and last week refused to sign off on a superseding complaint that added an obstruction charge against the two ex-officials."I'm concerned with your view as to what the law is," the judge told the prosecutors in a hearing last Tuesday. "Why today, on this one case, have you changed the entire history of how you charge cases?"

schema.headline: Judge tosses DOJ case against ex-FBI officials accused of lying about Hunter Biden probe

title: Connecticut Sen. Chris Murphy hospitalized after stroke, office says
description: Senate Appropriations Subcommittee on the Department of Homeland Security ranking member Sen. Chris Murphy (D-CT) quesitons U.S. Secretary of Homeland
body: Senate Appropriations Subcommittee on the Department of Homeland Security ranking member Sen. Chris Murphy (D-CT) quesitons U.S. Secretary of Homeland Security Markwayne Mullin during a heairng in the Dirksen Senate Office Building on Capitol Hill on June 02, 2026 in Washington, DC. Chip Somodevilla | Getty ImagesSen. Chris Murphy, a Connecticut Democrat, was hospitalized Saturday after suffering a stroke at his son's hockey game, his office announced on Sunday.Murphy is "awake and alert," according to a statement from his chief of staff, Allison Herwitt."Yesterday afternoon, Senator Murphy started experiencing numbness in his arm while at his son's hockey game. He was taken to a local hospital, where it was discovered he had experienced a stroke. He was transferred to Johns Hopkins for further monitoring and is responding well to treatment," Herwitt said.Johns Hopkins Hospital's main campus is in Baltimore, though it has other locations in and around Washington."The doctors are encouraged by his progress," Herwitt said. "We are optimistic he will make a full recovery."Murphy, who came to the Senate in 2013, is not up for reelection on Tuesday, but he's been crisscrossing the country campaigning for Democratic candidates, with recent stops in Michigan, Minnesota and Florida. He was due in New Hampshire on Sunday to campaign with Democratic Senate candidate Rep. Chris Pappas.He's seen as a potential 2028 presidential candidate and is a prolific Democratic fundraiser.Murphy, 53, spent six years in the House before running for the Senate. He rose to national prominence as an advocate for stricter gun control laws in the wake of the Sandy Hook shooting, which occurred in his home state. He's been a vocal critic of President Donald Trump and has opposed the war in Iran and the White House's deportation policies.He's one of multiple sitting senators to suffer a stroke in recent years. Democratic Sens. Ben Ray Luján of New Mexico and Chris Van Hollen of Maryland each had a stroke in 2022. And Sen. John Fetterman, D-Penn., who was then running for office, suffered a stroke just days before his state's Senate Democratic primary."Thinking of my great friend & colleague, Chris Murphy. I know how fiercely he fights & I'm certain I'll be welcoming him back to the Senate soon," Sen. Richard Blumenthal, a fellow Connecticut Democrat, posted to X on Sunday.

schema.headline: Connecticut Sen. Chris Murphy hospitalized after stroke, office says

title: Trump Account holders to receive SpaceX stock from Gwynne Shotwell in December
description: SpaceX President and Chief Operating Officer Gwynne Shotwell celebrates with family and other SpaceX employees at the Nasdaq Marketsite in New York af
body: SpaceX President and Chief Operating Officer Gwynne Shotwell celebrates with family and other SpaceX employees at the Nasdaq Marketsite in New York after the SpaceX initial public offering on June 12, 2026.Spencer Platt | Getty Images News | Getty ImagesEligible Trump Account holders will begin receiving donated shares of SpaceX stock next month, according to an X post on Friday."Robert and I are thrilled that our gift of over 2 million shares of SpaceX stock will be distributed to children's Trump accounts in December!" President and COO Gwynne Shotwell wrote in the post. The gift from Shotwell and her husband will provide a share apiece to around 2 million Trump Accounts holders ages 11 to 17 who live in ZIP codes with median family incomes of $57,000 or less, or in ZIP codes with too few residents for a median family income to be reported by the U.S. Census Bureau. These families should receive a notice by Monday, Shotwell wrote on X. "In a few weeks, an additional gift will be finalized for eligible 11 to 17-year-old children in military families serving overseas, children in foster care, and more children whose MFI is $90,000 or less living in counties near our home in the great state of Texas," she also wrote. Parents or guardians can check eligibility for the donation through Invest America, a nonprofit advocacy group, and track account activity with the Trump Accounts app.Read more CNBC personal finance coverageMidterm election: How affordability and the economy could affect voters' decisionsThese Senate races may help determine the fate of Social SecuritySocial Security: How much money beneficiaries may lose if Congress does nothingTrump Account holders to receive SpaceX stock from Gwynne Shotwell in DecemberCNBC's Financial Advisor 100: Best financial advisors, top firms for 2026 rankedCNBC Elite Advisors: Top ultra-high net worth wealth management firms for 2026Trump Accounts, also known as 530A accounts, are open to any U.S. child under 18 with a Social Security number.Children born from 2025 through 2028 may also receive a one-time $1,000 deposit from the U.S. Department of the Treasury. Other funds may also be available, depending on certain criteria. In a separate funding announcement in October, Elon Musk wrote in an X post that he plans to give every kid in America a share of SpaceX sometime in 2027, which may also come via Trump Accounts. The U.S. Department of the Treasury rolled out temporary regulations at the end of September that allow Trump Accounts to hold donated individual stocks, a change from previous guidelines that only allowed diversified, low-cost index funds.The move to permit stock donations could pave the way for more large-scale philanthropic gifts, Internal Revenue Service CEO Frank Bisignano told CNBC's "Squawk Box" on Oct. 8. On Oct. 29, Bisignano announced his own donation to Trump Accounts for eligible children ages 2 to 8 living in 11234, Bisignano's hometown ZIP code, according to The Bisignano Family Fund.

schema.headline: Trump Account holders to receive SpaceX stock from Gwynne Shotwell in December

title: Stock market after midterm elections: What S&P 500 history shows
description: watch nowMarkets are sweating it out ahead of the midterm elections, but the event historically heralds strong performance for stocks — regardless of
body: watch nowMarkets are sweating it out ahead of the midterm elections, but the event historically heralds strong performance for stocks — regardless of whether it's a red or blue wave, split decision, or status quo in Washington. The S&P 500 tends to perform well after both midterm and presidential elections. According to a CNBC analysis of S&P 500 returns after elections from 1980 through 2024, the index rose an average of 0.2% after one day and one week, and 1.1% after one month across both presidential and midterm elections.A year later, the index gained an average of 13.7% after midterms and 13.8% after presidential elections. Returns were positive in 91% of cases. And the S&P 500 was up after all 11 midterms from 1982 through 2022.Short-term returns were less reliable, particularly after presidential contests, which produced slightly negative average returns after one day and one week."There's some anxiousness before these elections," Ryan Detrick, CNBC contributor and chief market strategist at Carson Group, told CNBC. "Once you are through it, it's a big relief and markets tend to do pretty well."Markets prefer gridlockStill, the market usually prefers divided government: one party in charge of the White House and the other holding at least one house of Congress.Across 10 midterm and five presidential elections that left no single party in charge, the S&P 500 rose an average 15% after one year. One-year returns were positive in 14 out of 15 cases. By comparison, the index gained an average of 11.5% over the year after elections that resulted in single-party control."If you have a huge red wave or a big blue wave, markets actually kind of don't like that as much because you have too much spending one way and too much power," Detrick said. Leaving Democrats in control of Congress with a Republican in the White House — a scenario that may emerge from the elections on Tuesday — was also positive. A CNBC analysis found that after the three midterms (1986, 1990 and 2006) when Democrats controlled both houses and a Republican held the presidency, the S&P 500 averaged a 0.5% decline on the reaction day but was up 3.4% a month later and 10.9% after a year. Granted, elections may be coincident events to factors that matter far more for market performance. The S&P 500 plunged 22.1% in the year after the 2000 elections due to the dotcom bust, marking the worst post-election performance since 1980. Conversely, the S&P 500's best post-election year was a 38.3% gain after the 2020 elections, when markets mounted a massive comeback from the COVID-induced selloff.  Investors should bear in mind that Federal Reserve policy and the corporate earnings cycle ultimately matter more than elections, according to Société Générale.Stocks declined in the aftermath of the 2018 midterms, for instance, when Democrats wrested control of the House during President Donald Trump's first term. More importantly, the Fed tightened monetary policy that year, raising interest rates four times, and the S&P 500 ended the year down 6.2%, though the market was up 11.7% a year after the election.  The big swing factor now is AI and whether declines in tech will continue. As long as the AI wave is still moving and the economy keeps growing, "this bull market is probably still alive and well," Detrick says.But a Democratic sweep of the House and Senate would almost certainly pressure the AI infrastructure buildout and could lead to more retrenchment. The bond market is also skittish with yields rising globally and a mini debt crisis in France. And the war with Iran could get worse post-election if President Trump follows through on threats of more strikes or Iran escalates. "Seasonality isn't destiny, and worries around Iran, AI and France won't mysteriously vanish," said Jim Reid, Deutsche Bank's global head of macro and thematic research, in a note. If history is any guide, we could see a Santa rally and S&P 500 gains after the midterms. But this is still an AI-driven market, with geopolitics, the Fed, and bond market very much in charge. — CNBC's Chris Hayes contributed reporting.

schema.headline: Stock market after midterm elections: What S&P 500 history shows

title: Crude oil prices sell off more than 7% on Iran peace talk hopes ahead of U.S. midterms
description: watch nowCrude oil prices fell sharply Monday as the presidents of the U.S. and Iran signalled they are open to a diplomatic solution to the conflict
body: watch nowCrude oil prices fell sharply Monday as the presidents of the U.S. and Iran signalled they are open to a diplomatic solution to the conflict that has disrupted energy markets for eight months. U.S. West Texas Intermediate futures shed 7.4% to close at $96.46 a barrel, the biggest daily loss since July 27. Brent crude, the international benchmark, lost 7.6% to settle at $104.77 a barrel. President Donald Trump told reporters Monday that Iran wants to "make a deal and that could happen." U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio said over the weekend that Trump prefers not to use military force against Iran and would like to resolve the conflict diplomatically.Trump has previously said that he will not attack Iran before the U.S. midterms. But the oil market had priced in the risk of a major military escalation after the elections, gaining more than 10% in October. The oil market has sold off during previous phases of the war on rumors of a possible settlement, only for the conflict to subsequently escalate and spike prices again.Stock Chart IconStock chart icon Brent Trump "hasn't made a decision" on whether to strike Iran again, Rubio told reporters. "What the president expresses to you is incredible confidence that if we needed to do something militarily, we would have the ability to do it," the secretary of State said. "But we would prefer to do it peacefully." Iran's President Masoud Pezeshkian said Tehran is seeking to resolve problems through dialogue, according to state-owned Islamic Republic News Agency. Iran's Supreme Leader Ayatollah Mojtaba Khamenei has granted the government certain authorities to do this, Pezeshkian said.Iran's foreign minister, Abbas Araghchi, said an agreement with the U.S. is possible if Washington "demonstrates goodwill" and is "truly seeking a peaceful solution," according to IRNA.Araghchi said mediators are discussing the proposal Iran made during the United Nations General Assembly in September. Tehran expects the U.S. to lift sanctions, reduce its military presence in the region to previous levels and lift the blockade, the foreign minister said. Stock Chart IconStock chart icon wtiBut Khamenei on Saturday called for Tehran's armed forces to meet "any level or type of threat" with "an immediate, impactful, and geographically unrestricted response."Reports about diplomatic efforts will have a big impact on crude oil prices because much of the market's recent gains were risk premium in anticipation of a possible escalation, according to Ryan McKay, director of commodity strategy at TD Securities. "With that said, so long as there is no concrete conclusion to the war, and tanker and Houthi attacks remain prevalent, we do not anticipate a complete erosion of the risk premium via diplomacy headlines alone," McKay said. — CNBC's Lim Hui Jie contributed to this report.

schema.headline: Crude oil prices sell off more than 7% on Iran peace talk hopes ahead of U.S. midterms

title: Social Security may have to cut retirement benefits in six years. Here's how much money is at stake for beneficiaries
description: Maryvit Luna - CNBC | Getty imagesSocial Security retirement benefits may face an automatic, across-the-board cut in just six years.Without interventi
body: Maryvit Luna - CNBC | Getty imagesSocial Security retirement benefits may face an automatic, across-the-board cut in just six years.Without intervention before then, the Social Security retirement trust fund, formally known as the Old-Age and Survivors Insurance Trust Fund, which helps pay benefits to eligible workers and qualifying family members, will run out in the fourth quarter of 2032, the program's trustees said in a June report.At that time, the trustees project retirement benefits will be cut by 22%.The Congressional Budget Office has a more dire forecast, anticipating that the retirement trust fund may run out sooner, in mid-2032, and that retirees may see larger benefit cuts, at 26%, upon insolvency. Beneficiaries may receive an average $500 cut to their monthly benefits across the U.S. based on a 24% benefit reduction, according to a June report from the Committee for a Responsible Federal Budget. In 29 states, retirees would see even bigger average reductions, according to the nonpartisan organization focused on educating the public on fiscal policy issues. Senators elected this November will be in office in 2032, when the retirement trust fund depletion date hits. Their ability to right the ship is crucial for retirees and the economy. But it's not a sure thing given the political climate inside the beltway."The attention on 2032 is appropriate in the sense that that is when beneficiaries and future beneficiaries will see and feel the consequences of inaction," said Shai Akabas, vice president of economic policy at the Bipartisan Policy Center, a public policy think tank focused on promoting bipartisan cooperation."Nothing gets Congress to move like that type of deadline," he said.Of course, brinksmanship and political deadlock may stymie efforts. Congress could opt to kick the can down the road, rather than enact changes to shore up Social Security — which may require tax increases, benefit cuts or a combination of both.If lawmakers decide to combine Social Security's retirement and disability trust funds, the depletion date may move to the third quarter of 2034, when benefits may be cut by 17%, according to Social Security's trustees.Akabas said any delay by lawmakers would have consequences: Social Security's shortfall would continue to increase. There could also be consequences for the economy, he said.In 2023, Social Security benefits generated $2.6 trillion in total economic output and supported more than 12 million jobs, according to 2025 research by the National Institute on Retirement Security, a Washington, D.C., based nonprofit, nonpartisan organization.A 19% benefit cut could reduce gross domestic product by hundreds of billions of dollars, according to the NIRS research.Moreover, failing to muster Social Security reform would prompt bond market strain, according to research published in June by George Mason University's Mercatus Center. Social Security is tied to the bond market because its trust funds are invested in special issue U.S. Treasury bonds. If Social Security reform is delayed, that may put upward pressure on Treasury yields, with investors wanting higher returns for long-term bonds. Delayed reform may either prompt higher interest rates and borrowing costs or inflationary adjustments that hurt the value of government liabilities, according to the Mercatus Center research. Those changes may affect household budgets through higher borrowing costs for mortgages, auto loans and other types of consumer credit as well as student loans, according to the research. If interest rates and prices rise, that will interfere with economic growth, Akabas said."Those effects are also ones that the American people feel, in addition to adjustments to their benefits," Akabas said.Heading to the midterms, some Democratic congressional candidates have said they would raise or eliminate the Social Security payroll tax cap so high earners pay more into the program. In 2026, the 6.2% tax paid by both workers and their employers applies to earnings up to $184,500.Yet it remains to be seen whether Washington leaders will have the political will to address the problem soon. Tax increases, in particular, may not be viewed as politically popular heading into the 2028 presidential election.As such, payroll taxes are "extraordinarily unlikely" to rise in the next couple of years, said Jessica Riedl, a fellow at the Urban-Brookings Tax Policy Center, which provides independent analyses of tax issues. If those tax hikes happen, it would likely be closer to 2032, she said."In Washington, they love to wait until the last minute," Riedl said. "There's no interest on either side for these sorts of tax increases in the short term. In the long term, I think everything is on the table."The National Committee to Preserve Social Security and Medicare, founded by President Franklin D. Roosevelt's son, former U.S. Rep. James Roosevelt, has scored incumbent lawmakers on whether their votes have protected those programs.The advocacy organization has also endorsed candidates who support raising payroll taxes and protecting Social Security benefits from cuts. With those endorsements, the NCPSSM gives candidates a set of boxing gloves as a symbol of the fights they'll face in Congress, according to Dan Adcock, the NCPSSM's director of government relations and policy.The organization is also working to educate voters that the senators elected this year will be among those to deal with Social Security, he said."We've been trying to impress upon voters why this is an issue that should be top tier," Adcock said. "They need to be asking candidates about what their plans for the program would be."
